title: Why Would Anyone Live in Oymyakon? I Tried.
question: Why do people live in Oymyakon?
message: This video tells curious adults that the coldest village on Earth grew around water that would not freeze, and that the cold was the price of staying, not the reason to come.
angle: People live in Oymyakon because reindeer herders stopped at warm springs that stayed open all winter and that stopping place grew into a village a Soviet weather station later made famous, despite January averages around minus forty-six Celsius and only about four and a half hours of December sun.

scenes.narration: This is a fish. I bought it in Oymyakon, often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth. Roughly five hundred people live there. Why would anyone choose that?

scenes.narration: I didn't go as a tourist. I went to move in. I packed a toothbrush, a scarf, and a paper map. The map was upside down for most of the trip. My plan was simple. Find the chilliest village anyone has heard of, live there, and get famous for being cold. By the end of the trip, I knew why people really live there. It isn't the cold. It's something that refused to be cold. I also knew whether I was unpacking.

On paper, it's one short dotted line. In real life, the dotted line has opinions. My backpack didn't fit under the seat, so it sat on my lap, and I sat under it. Outside the window, snow went by. Then more snow. Then a very small sign.

scenes.narration: I arrived in late December. Around then, the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day. I arrived during one of the hours it wasn't. January averages around minus forty-six Celsius. That's about minus fifty-one Fahrenheit. The sign at the edge of the village was very small. So was the village. I stepped out to take a photo of the sign. My eyelashes froze. I didn't know I had eyelashes. My camera took one look at the weather and switched itself off.

scenes.narration: Standing by that tiny sign, I had a question. Why is there a village here at all? Somebody picked this spot, on purpose. I had guesses. My first guess was the view. It was dark. My second guess was fishing. I tapped the river with a stick. The river tapped back. My third guess was that nobody checked the weather before moving in. I liked my third guess. My third guess was wrong.

scenes.narration: Turns out the answer was hiding in the name. Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze. Linguists argue about the roots. Some sources trace the word to the Even language, while others point to Sakha. But the story told about this valley is the same. Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter. So I went looking for one. I walked past it twice. It was steaming. I was reading my map. My map was upside down.

scenes.role: cơ chế thật: người chăn tuần lộc dừng ở suối, điểm dừng thành làng
scenes.narration: Picture a single gas station on an empty highway, at night, in a blizzard. You don't stop there because it's pretty. Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys. If you move reindeer across a frozen landscape, open water isn't a curiosity. It's the whole point. A stopping place became a regular camp. Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village. So the village didn't appear despite the cold. It appeared because, in the middle of all that cold, something refused to freeze. I dipped my water bottle into the spring. For once, it sloshed.

scenes.role: chương 3: Wob thử đứng ở chỗ lạnh nhất; đài Pole of Cold, kỷ lục 1933, Verkhoyansk
scenes.narration: Next, I went to find the chilliest spot in town. That was the whole point of the move. Oymyakon has a monument for it, the Pole of Cold, so I stood next to it and tried to look famous. Why a monument? Because the record that made Oymyakon famous came from the local weather station in nineteen thirty-three. On the sixth of February, it recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That's about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight. So even the number comes with an argument. Either way, it's the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost. Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number. Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed. I measured the distance on my map with my fingers. I decided Verkhoyansk could keep its half.

scenes.role: cú lật: trạm đo nằm giữa Oymyakon và Tomtor; trạm và sân bay thời Xô viết
scenes.narration: Then it got complicated. The weather station behind that famous number isn't in Oymyakon itself. It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield. The station and the airfield both date from the Soviet era. Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument. So a village got famous partly because someone finally put a thermometer nearby. Thermometers are very good at making places famous. I went to the station. Then back to the monument. Then I tried standing exactly halfway, so I could live in both. Halfway turned out to be mostly frozen road.

scenes.role: hiểu ra: vì sao lạnh vậy (áp cao Siberia, thung lũng như cái bát)
scenes.narration: Lying on that road, I finally asked a better question. Why is it this cold here at all? Oymyakon isn't even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it. The reason is boring and brilliant. In winter, a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space. Then there's the valley. Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor. So the cold isn't a spot. It's the whole bowl. I thought about climbing out. Up there it's warmer. Up there it's also a mountain. I stayed in the bowl.

scenes.role: lịch sử nghiêm túc: Gulag Kolyma và đường Kolyma; không gag
scenes.narration: I'm going to put the fish down for this part. The same era brought something much darker to this region. In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold. Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties. Many of them did not survive. The village's story begins with the springs. But the highway that crosses this region was built by people who had no choice.

scenes.narration: Back in the village, I tried to get through one ordinary day. Morning. Still dark. Outside, a car sat in the street with its engine running and nobody in it. Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting, because a frozen engine may refuse to start at all. Think of your car on a winter morning. Now imagine the winter never gives back the keys. I patted the car on the hood, like a horse. The car kept running. It had places to be.

scenes.narration: Midday, I went to the market. Food here comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible. I asked for a bag. The fish did not need a bag. The fish could stand up on its own. That's when it clicked. In winter, the village itself is the freezer. I carried my fish home on my shoulder, like a plank. Yes. This fish.

scenes.narration: Afternoon. I needed a bathroom. Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets. I looked at the path to the outhouse for a long time. I made a decision. I waited. On the way back, I passed the school. According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two. The exact cut-off for each age group depends on who you ask. Plenty of schools elsewhere close for a light dusting of snow. I asked whether Oymyakon has snow days. It does. They're just extremely specific.

I sat by the window with my scarf, my upside-down map, and a fish that was clearly handling this better than me. The fish had made peace with everything. I had not. That night, I started packing.

scenes.role: chương 6: quay lại tháng Bảy; kỷ lục nóng 2010, biên độ ~102 độ; Wob đổi ý lần 2
scenes.narration: And yet, I went back in July. Partly out of stubbornness. Mostly to see whether the village had a second personality. It does. I'd just missed the long days. By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours. In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That's about ninety-four Fahrenheit. Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth have record highs and lows that far apart. I had packed the same bag. Everything in it was fur. And for one sweaty afternoon, I wanted to move in again.

scenes.narration: Then I met the residents who never go inside. Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter. A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats. Imagine buying the right jacket, except your body grows the jacket for you. My only adaptation is a large backpack. I tried to make friends with one. The horse kept eating. The horse has seen tourists before.

scenes.narration: I had also missed the party. Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor. Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence. In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here. In the cold. On purpose. So the water brought the herders, the thermometer brought the fame, and now the cold itself brings visitors. A village that grew up around water that wouldn't freeze now welcomes people because of everything that does.

scenes.narration: So here's what my desk knows now. The cold was never the reason to come. It was the price of staying. Would I move there? The springs are lovely. The summer surprised me. But the winters are long, dark and brutally cold, and I lasted about one cup of tea. My verdict is NOPE. That valley is for people who grew up with it, or who truly love winter: silence, clear skies, and a summer that feels earned. The fish lives in my freezer now. It's the warmest winter it has ever had. One January there, for one July. Would you take that trade?

verdict.label: NOPE

claims.quote: My eyelashes froze.
claims.statement: In winter in Oymyakon, Russia, temperatures are cold enough that people's eyelashes freeze outdoors and residents often leave car engines running for long periods so they will restart.

claims.quote: Roughly five hundred people live there.
claims.statement: The village of Oymyakon in the Sakha Republic, Russia, has roughly 500 permanent residents (462 in the 2010 Russian census).

claims.quote: often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth
claims.statement: Oymyakon is often described as the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth.

claims.quote: On the sixth of February, it recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That's about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight.
claims.statement: On 6 February 1933 the weather station at Oymyakon, Russia, recorded about minus 68 degrees Celsius (about minus 90 Fahrenheit); Guinness World Records lists the value as minus 67.7 C and the World Meteorological Organization lists minus 67.8 C.

claims.quote: Either way, it's the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's 1933 reading is the lowest recorded temperature for a permanently inhabited place, though Verkhoyansk has a comparable reading and some sources treat the record as shared.

claims.quote: Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number.
claims.statement: Verkhoyansk, Russia, northwest of Oymyakon, recorded a temperature of about minus 67.7 to minus 67.8 degrees Celsius in February 1892.

claims.quote: Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed.
claims.statement: Some sources (for example Guinness World Records) describe Oymyakon and Verkhoyansk as sharing the record low for an inhabited place, while the World Meteorological Organization lists only Oymyakon and treats the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed.

claims.quote: It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield.
claims.statement: The weather station associated with Oymyakon's temperature records is located in a valley between the villages of Oymyakon and Tomtor, near the airfield at Tomtor, rather than in Oymyakon village itself.

claims.quote: Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument.
claims.statement: Some sources argue that the nearby village of Tomtor, where the record was measured, is the real Pole of Cold, while the official Pole of Cold monument stands in Oymyakon.

claims.quote: Oymyakon isn't even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it.
claims.statement: Oymyakon (about 63.5 degrees north) lies south of the Arctic Circle (about 66.5 degrees north).

claims.quote: In winter, a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space.
claims.statement: In winter, the Siberian High, a semi-permanent area of high pressure, sits over eastern Siberia, bringing clear, dry, stable air that allows strong radiative cooling of the ground around Oymyakon.

claims.quote: Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's valley setting traps dense cold air near the valley floor (a temperature inversion), and studies have found that in winter the surrounding mountain slopes can be much warmer than the valley floor.

claims.quote: Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze.
claims.statement: The name Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning unfrozen or non-freezing water.

claims.quote: Some sources trace the word to the Even language, while others point to Sakha.
claims.statement: Sources disagree on the origin of the name Oymyakon: some derive it from the Even language (for example the word kheium), others from the Sakha (Yakut) language.

claims.quote: Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter.
claims.statement: There are warm or thermal springs near Oymyakon whose water does not freeze in winter.

claims.quote: Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys.
claims.statement: Reindeer herders historically stopped at the springs near Oymyakon to water their reindeer and rest.

claims.quote: A stopping place became a regular camp. Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village.
claims.statement: Over time, the herders' stopping place at Oymyakon grew into a permanent village.

claims.quote: The station and the airfield both date from the Soviet era.
claims.statement: During the Soviet period a weather station was established near Oymyakon and an airfield was built near the village of Tomtor.

claims.quote: the record that made Oymyakon famous came from the local weather station in nineteen thirty-three
claims.statement: Oymyakon's fame as the coldest inhabited place rests largely on the minus 67.7 degrees Celsius reading taken at its weather station in 1933.

claims.quote: In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold.
claims.statement: In the 1930s the Soviet Union built a network of Gulag forced labour camps across the Kolyma region of north-eastern Siberia, largely for gold mining.

claims.quote: Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties.
claims.statement: Construction of the Kolyma Highway began in the early 1930s using Gulag prisoner labour, and forced labour was used on it into the 1950s.

claims.quote: Many of them did not survive.
claims.statement: Many of the prisoners who built the Kolyma Highway died during its construction.

claims.quote: January averages around minus forty-six Celsius. That's about minus fifty-one Fahrenheit.
claims.statement: The average January temperature at Oymyakon is around minus 46 degrees Celsius.

claims.quote: Around then, the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day.
claims.statement: Around the December solstice, Oymyakon gets roughly four and a half hours of daylight per day.

claims.quote: Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets.
claims.statement: Oymyakon sits on permafrost, which makes conventional water pipes difficult to maintain, and many homes there use outdoor toilets.

claims.quote: Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting, because a frozen engine may refuse to start at all.
claims.statement: In Oymyakon, cars are often left running for long periods or warmed with a fire before starting, because engines may not start in extreme cold.

claims.quote: Food here comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible.
claims.statement: The diet in Oymyakon relies heavily on meat and fish, fish is sold frozen in winter, and farming is very difficult because of the frozen ground.

claims.quote: According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two. The exact cut-off for each age group depends on who you ask.
claims.statement: In the Oymyakonsky district of Yakutia, classes for younger schoolchildren are cancelled when the temperature falls to around minus 52 degrees Celsius; exact thresholds for different ages vary between reports.

claims.quote: By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours.
claims.statement: From around mid-June to the solstice, daylight at Oymyakon lasts more than 20 hours per day.

claims.quote: In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That's about ninety-four Fahrenheit.
claims.statement: Oymyakon's weather station recorded a high of 34.6 degrees Celsius (about 94 Fahrenheit) in July 2010.

claims.quote: Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth have record highs and lows that far apart.
claims.statement: The difference between Oymyakon's record low (minus 67.7 C) and record high (34.6 C) is about 102 degrees Celsius, one of the largest temperature ranges of any place on Earth.

claims.quote: Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter.
claims.statement: Yakutian horses in the Sakha Republic live outdoors all year round, including through the winter.

claims.quote: A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats.
claims.statement: A 2015 genomic study (Librado et al., PNAS) found that Yakutian horses descend from domestic horses brought to the region a few centuries ago and adapted to the subarctic cold very quickly, with compact bodies and very hairy winter coats.

claims.quote: Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor.
claims.statement: A festival called Pole of Cold (Journey to the Pole of Cold) is held each spring in the Oymyakonsky district, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor.

claims.quote: Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence.
claims.statement: Chyskhaan, the Lord of Cold in Sakha (Yakut) tradition, is a central figure of the Pole of Cold festival and has an ice residence associated with him.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here.
claims.statement: A marathon called Pole of Cold - Oymyakon was held in the Oymyakon area in 2025.
